youtube.baslik: Who Is a Hearing Aid Candidate? Needs Assessment | Lesson 188 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Hearing aid candidacy is not decided by the audiogram alone. In this lesson we cover audiological findings, speech-in-noise testing, situations that call for medical referral, motivation and expectations, and setting personal goals with the COSI.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Dillon, James and Ginis (1997), Client Oriented Scale of Improvement (COSI), Journal of the American Academy of Audiology; American Academy of Audiology, Guidelines for the Audiologic Management of Adult Hearing Impairment; Cox and Alexander (2000), Expectations about hearing aids (ECHO); Social Security Institution, Health Implementation Communiqué (SUT), Türkiye, section on hearing aids and earmolds.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how we assess when a person is likely to benefit from a hearing aid.
We will look at findings, needs, motivation, expectations, and goal setting with the Client Oriented Scale of Improvement, or COSI.
Hearing aid candidacy is the assessment of how likely a person is to gain meaningful benefit from a hearing aid.
Clinical guidelines do not give a single decibel cutoff for candidacy.
Of two people with the same audiogram, one may struggle every day while the other has no marked difficulty.
What decides is how much the loss affects the person's communication and participation in life.
So someone with a mild loss who sits in meetings all day at work can also be a strong candidate.
In the end, the decision is made together with the person, weighing the findings and their needs.
We can think of the needs assessment as resting on four pillars.
The first is the audiological findings: thresholds, speech understanding and performance in noise.
The second is communication needs: where, with whom and in which situations does the person struggle?
The third is motivation and expectations: who wants the hearing aid, and what is expected of it?
The fourth is factors that affect hearing aid use, such as dexterity, vision and cognitive status.
The assessment begins with the history in the person's own words; if possible, a family member is also heard.
Next come pure-tone and speech audiometry; a speech-in-noise test is also very valuable at this stage.
Self-report questionnaires, such as the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly (HHIE), show what the difficulty means to the person.
Then the person's most important communication goals are identified and written down.
In the last step, all findings are shared with the person and the options, including hearing aids, are discussed together.
This approach is called shared decision making, and it increases hearing aid uptake.
In this example, the right ear shows a mild to moderately severe loss that increases toward the high frequencies.
Bone conduction thresholds are close to air conduction, so the loss is sensorineural.
The left ear has a loss of a similar degree; the two ears are close to each other, that is, symmetrical.
This person usually understands face-to-face conversation in quiet but misses high-frequency consonants.
A symmetrical bilateral loss is a typical example for fitting hearing aids in both ears.
However, the audiogram does not tell us how much the person struggles in noise or whether they want a hearing aid.
Speech-in-noise tests show how much a person struggles in noise, independent of the audiogram.

cumleler.yazi: The Quick Speech-in-Noise test, or QuickSIN, reports the result as signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, loss; 0 to 3 dB is near normal.

cumleler: 3 to 7 dB is a mild SNR loss; these people may perform close to normal listeners in noise.
7 to 15 dB is moderate; noise-oriented features such as directional microphones become important.
With a loss above 15 dB, additional systems such as a remote microphone may be needed.
This result is also a powerful counseling tool for discussing what can be expected in noise.
Before recommending a hearing aid, conditions that need medical evaluation must be ruled out.
Chief among them are a sudden or rapidly progressing loss and an unexplained one-sided or asymmetric loss.
If there is ear discharge, pain or bleeding, a physician's evaluation is needed first.
New or ongoing dizziness is also a reason for referral to a physician.
A marked air-bone gap may point to a treatable conductive problem.
A malformation of the pinna or ear canal, impacted wax or a foreign body is also assessed by a physician first.
To understand motivation, the first question is simple: does the person want the aid, or does their family?
A person who comes at the insistence of relatives and does not accept their own difficulty is more likely to stop using the aid.
The person can be asked to mark on a zero to ten scale how important it is for them to do something about their hearing.
According to the stages of change model, the person may still be contemplating; then information and time come first.
Rather than selling a hearing aid to someone who is not ready, planning the next visit is often the better choice.
Stigma concerns and cost also affect motivation; discussing them openly builds trust.
Expectations are among the factors that most strongly affect satisfaction with hearing aids.
A hearing aid does not restore normal hearing; the person should know this from the very start.
Benefit may be more limited in noisy settings than in quiet ones.
The brain may take a few weeks to get used to new sounds; in the first days, sounds may seem artificial and noisy.
The hearing aid needs daily cleaning, charging or batteries, and regular check-ups.

cumleler.yazi: Expectations can also be explored before fitting with the Expected Consequences of Hearing aid Ownership scale, or ECHO.

cumleler: The Client Oriented Scale of Improvement, or COSI, was developed in Australia.
The person names up to five specific situations in which they struggle because of their hearing and want to improve.
The situations are written not in general terms but concretely, in the person's own words.
These goals are then ranked by their importance to the person.
After hearing aid use, two questions are asked for each goal: how much has it changed, and how often do you succeed now?
This way success is measured not by the audiogram but by the situations the person cares about.
The change question has five options: worse, no difference, slightly better, better and much better.
Current ability is also given in five levels, corresponding to 10, 25, 50, 75 and 95 percent of the time.
In this example, the person is better off when watching television with their spouse and succeeds most of the time.
There is only slight improvement in the team meeting; this goal gives a clue for fine-tuning and additional solutions.
The phone goal, on the other hand, is much better, with success almost all the time.
A table like this gives a concrete basis for discussing the next steps with the person.

maddeler.metin: Medical board report with an ENT specialist
Four-frequency average of at least 26 dB
A payment rule, not candidacy criterion

cumleler: In Türkiye, for the Social Security Institution to cover the cost of a hearing aid, a medical board report is required.
The report is issued at an official health institution, and the board includes at least one ear, nose and throat specialist.
The air conduction average at 500, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz must be at least 26 dB in the ear concerned.
From age eight, a speech discrimination test is also required; under age four, electrophysiological and behavioral tests are used.
Under the regulation, audiological test results are valid for 6 months.
These criteria are a condition for payment; clinical candidacy rests on the broader assessment we saw above.
These rules can be updated as the regulation changes; in practice, always check the current regulation.

sahneler.metin: Write COSI goals concretely, in the person's own words: not "understanding in noise" but "talking with my daughter at a café on Saturday evenings". A concrete goal is measurable.
cumleler: A tip from the field: write COSI goals as concretely as possible.
With a general goal such as understanding in noise, it is hard to judge whether things have improved.
A goal such as talking with my daughter at a café on Saturday evenings also shows you what to focus on in fine-tuning.
Writing the goal in the person's own words increases their involvement in and ownership of the process.
Opening the same sheet together at the follow-up visit lets you share progress with the person in concrete terms.

maddeler.metin: Candidacy is more than the audiogram
Rule out reasons for medical referral
COSI: up to five personal goals

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that candidacy is decided not by a single decibel cutoff but by communication difficulty and likely benefit.
Before a hearing aid, conditions that need referral to a physician must be ruled out.
Motivation and realistic expectations are among the strongest predictors of hearing aid success.
The COSI makes it possible to set goals with up to five situations chosen by the person and to track the outcome.

sahneler.soru: In the COSI, how many goals can the person set at most?
sahneler.aciklama: In the COSI the person chooses up to _five specific situations_ and ranks them by importance.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: on the COSI, what is the maximum number of communication goals a person sets?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: five.
The person chooses up to five specific situations, ranks them, and at follow-up rates the change and current ability for each.
